marble.name: Solids, Liquids & Gases
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Compare and group materials as solids, liquids, or gases based on their observable properties and behaviour
marble.prompt: Can you explain the difference between a solid like ice, a liquid like water, and a gas like steam, and sort everyday things into these three groups?

cluster.summary: Your child is exploring the materials around them — identifying different substances like wood, plastic, and metal, and discovering their properties such as whether they're hard or soft, rough or smooth.

misconceptions: Sorting by appearance — anything that pours (sand, salt, powder) is called a liquid, missing that each grain is a solid.
Gases are not matter / are weightless / are 'nothing', because they are usually invisible ('seeing is believing').
Believing the visible white cloud of 'steam' IS the water vapour, rather than tiny condensed droplets (the true vapour is invisible).
Thinking a liquid changes amount when it changes container shape (confusing shape with quantity).
Assuming very thick liquids (honey, gel) or very light solids (foam) can't be classified, or classifying them by feel rather than behaviour.
representations: A three-behaviour test chart (keeps shape / fills container / fills all space)
A same-liquid-in-different-containers demonstration (shape changes, amount stays)
Tricky-case cards: sand/powder (pours but solid), steam (gas vs droplets), honey, foam
A trapped-air bag / bubble demo making a gas observable
An eight-plus material sort with behaviour justifications
authoredAnswer: Sand is a SOLID: it's made of many tiny solid grains, each keeping its shape; the pile pours only because the grains slide over one another. The white cloud above a kettle is NOT the gas — true steam (water vapour) is invisible; the white cloud is tiny liquid droplets that have condensed as the vapour cooled.
probe: With the teacher handling a kettle safely, boil it and point out the small CLEAR gap right at the spout before the white cloud begins. wrongAnswers.wrong: Sand is a liquid because it pours and takes the shape of the bucket.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Calls sand, sugar or salt a liquid.
wrongAnswers.fix: Examine one grain under a magnifier — a hard solid with a fixed shape; contrast the pouring PILE with the fixed GRAIN.

wrongAnswers.wrong: The white cloud above the kettle is the gas — that's what steam looks like.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Points at the kettle plume (or breath on a cold day) as 'the gas'.
wrongAnswers.fix: Note the clear gap just above the spout (that's the invisible vapour); the white cloud further up is where it has cooled into tiny liquid droplets.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Says a gas isn't a material, or that a sealed 'empty' bottle contains nothing.
wrongAnswers.fix: Fan the air, squeeze a sealed bottle, weigh an inflated vs deflated ball — gases are real matter that take up space and have mass.
